[{:db/id 17592186398514 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x+y,\,2x-y,\,x+z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2u-2v} \\  & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,u+(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,3u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,3u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u+v)\cdot (-2)+(2u-v)\cdot (2)+(3u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u-2v+4u-2v+3u-2v \\  & =5u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x+y,\,2x-y,\,x+z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5u-6v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}(5u-6v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186398521 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$

$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)v\cdot (-1)+(u-v)u\cdot (1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-uv+{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}-uv+uv \\  & ={u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278510 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$

$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1\}.

$$

$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y-z,\,x+y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-2v} \\  & =⟨u,\,v-(u-2v),\,u+v⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\,3v-u,\,u+v⟩\end{aligned}

1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y-z,\,x+y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-2v} \\  & =⟨u,\,v-(u-2v),\,u+v⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\,3v-u,\,u+v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,3v-u,\,u+v⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-1)+(3v-u)\cdot 2+(u+v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-u+6v-2u+u+v \\  & =-2u+7v.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x,\,y-z,\,x+y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2u+7v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2u+7v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}

y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 2}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x+y,\,2x-y,\,x+z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2u-2v} \\  & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,u+(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,3u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,3u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u+v)\cdot (-2)+(2u-v)\cdot (2)+(3u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u-2v+4u-2v+3u-2v \\  & =5u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x+y,\,2x-y,\,x+z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5u-6v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}(5u-6v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186398521 :question/id #uuid "d5e1155b-c484-5f31-a815-946d2d63d6df" :question/math-academy-id "q-161359" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198389 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a3486150-b3c2-5faf-99d5-b42ced350996" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c8c22e69-9068-5d72-8593-ce78861036f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398523} {:answer/id #uuid "2f4db3f6-9c97-526b-8cb2-065c8f5de466" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398524} {:answer/id #uuid "7b2e8a80-65c9-5d70-9b0e-0e801e7e718d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(u+v)^{2}" :db/id 17592186398525} {:answer/id #uuid "9f182d4d-0129-52ff-90b2-56e5acb487b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(u-v)^{2}" :db/id 17592186398526} {:answer/id #uuid "c1e4fd3a-37bb-5bcd-85c6-185c9a1d61c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{u}^{2}+uv-{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398527}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c8c22e69-9068-5d72-8593-ce78861036f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398523} :answer-field/id #uuid "396da9a4-de3b-5bd7-8b5e-dfc780e10bb9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186398522}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

17592186199282}} {:db/id 17592186199300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199470 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive a general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Consider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle.
$$

Computing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the $\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize as follows:

- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$

- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - R\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf j$-component is positive.*

- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( P - Q\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "d20203b0-e15f-5061-ae68-16676ec933dc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7653 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Flux Over Cartesian Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "299c6f48-c761-519a-8d96-161fea9d6df0" :step/math-academy-id 44449 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199299}} {:db/id 17592186199306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199473 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate the flux of the vector field

$$

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: 2v-2u \right\rangle

$$

$$

=

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨(x-y)^{2},\,(x+y)^{2},\,12xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}4uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =[{u}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =({1}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot ({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Consider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle.
$$

Computing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the $\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize as follows:

- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$

- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - R\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf j$-component is positive.*

- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( P - Q\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "d20203b0-e15f-5061-ae68-16676ec933dc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7653 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Flux Over Cartesian Surfaces"} {:db/id 17592186199473 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=\left\langle (x-y)^2, \:(x+y)^2, \: 12xy \right\rangle
$$

 

through the surface $S$ defined by the Cartesian equation 

$$
z=2y-2x
$$

for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ 

For surfaces like this, substituting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain a parametrization 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: 2v-2u \right\rangle
$$

over the domain 

$$
D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 1, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

 

Recall that for a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨(x-y)^{2},\,(x+y)^{2},\,12xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2v-2u} \\  & =⟨(u-v)^{2},\,(u+v)^{2},\,12uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)^{2},\,(u+v)^{2},\,12uv⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)^{2}\cdot 2+(u+v)^{2}\cdot (-2)+12uv\cdot 1 \\  & =4uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨(x-y)^{2},\,(x+y)^{2},\,12xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}4uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =[{u}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =({1}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot ({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f32d6993-cd62-5fe7-98f3-9a89a815dbfc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7666 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} {:course/id #uuid These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
